However, it relies on quite a few attitudes, dispositions, and behaviors among the voters to be an accurate depiction of the events.

For instance, voters are not obligated--after throwing in with a more popular candidate (party) than their chosen candidate (party) in a given election--to maintain those temporary allegiances in future elections. Voters also have to be convinced (in the U.S. this has been accomplished through media and post-election shaming, à la Nader) that not falling in line with one of the two "strongest" parties is a pointless and pernicious endeavor. It is not. Parties have to form and maintain these coalitions of voting blocks.

If the parties can keep their various constituent groups satisfied, a two-party system can survive. What you're seeing in the U.S. right now is what happens when they cannot keep all of their constituent groups satisfied.
